docs.title: Software Development Pathway
docs.text:
Notes and code for the Digital Technology — Software Development pathway at Walker Career Center, Warren Central High School.

This site holds the slides and the code. Canvas holds everything else — your assignments, the daily agenda on the calendar, and the gradebook. If you are looking for something to turn in, it is in Canvas.

Every course runs on the Black/Gold block schedule, so each lesson below lists the days it is taught for both cohorts. Lessons that have not been written yet still appear, so you can see where the course is going.

docs.title: Course Orientation & Self-Guided Model
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · Orient Orientation · Module 0

Scheduled Black Fri, Jul 31, 2026 · Gold Mon, Aug 3, 2026

🎯 Objective

By the end of orientation you can:

  • Explain how this self-guided course works — modules, check-ins, the notes
  • Describe the year's arc: JavaScript → React → a deployed app of your own
  • Have VS Code and Node.js running, and use javascript.info to find answers yourself
Welcome to the capstone

You've been through the pathway — you've shipped games in Godot, built websites and databases, and written Java and Python. This course is different: you drive. There are no daily lectures. Instead you work through structured modules at your own pace, and we meet in short check-ins where you show me what you built and explain how it works.

That's the whole model, and it's how real developers actually learn: pick up a new tool, work the docs, build something, and be able to explain it. This year that tool is React — the industry-standard library for building web applications — and the language underneath it, modern JavaScript.

The arc — where this goes Half What you do Part 1 — JavaScript for React (≈ first half) Master the modern JavaScript React is written in — functions, array methods, ES6+, classes, data structures, async. Build a vanilla-JS data app. Part 2 — React.js (≈ second half) Rebuild that app in React, then expand it into your capstone — deployed, and presented.

By December you'll have a real React application, live on the internet, that you designed and can send anyone. That's the capstone.

How a module works

Every module follows the same shape — learn it once:

🎯 Objective     what you'll be able to do
📖 Learn         the resources to work through (javascript.info, react.dev, MDN)
⌨️  Practice      exercises with success criteria you can check yourself
🔨 Build         apply it to your project
✅ Check yourself can you do it without looking?
🏁 Done when      you submit it — demo it and explain it

The 🏁 build check is the assessment. You show me the working code and explain every line. When you can, the module's done. If you can't yet, no penalty — you revise and resubmit. Mastery is the goal, not speed.

How you're graded Category Weight Project 01 40% Part 1 Project (Data App) 20% Part 2 Capstone (React App) 30% notes 10%

You're graded on what you can demonstrate and explain, not on seat time. Finish early and go deeper, or take the full time — both can earn top marks.

The rules
  • You own every line. The one rule that never bends. If you can't explain a line, it doesn't count — that's what the build check checks.
  • AI is allowed here — unlike the earlier pathway courses. You're advanced, you're headed into a field that uses these tools daily, and learning to supervise them is part of the course. Two conditions: disclose your use in your notes (what you asked, what you changed), and be able to explain everything you submit.
  • Keep your notes. One entry per module: what you built, one thing that confused you and how you fixed it, and any AI use. It's 10% of your grade and it's how you (and I) track where you are.
  • Deploy your projects. Real, public URLs. Publishing working software is the point.
Set up your tools (rolls into Module 1)
  1. Install Node.js (LTS) from nodejs.org. Verify: node --version.
  2. Open VS Code — same editor as the rest of the pathway. Make a capstone folder and open it. Ctrl+` opens a terminal already inside it.
  3. Bookmark: javascript.info and react.dev. These are where the content lives — there is no lecture coming.
  4. Make your capstone repo — on GitHub, with a notes.md at the root. One repo, all year: code, written work, and reflections.
🏁 Done when

Your environment runs, your notes is shared, the six-question reference drill is answered with URLs, and warmup.js runs. Check in with me — and be ready to explain warmup.js line by line. Then you're into Module 1.

Next: Part 1, Module 1 — JS Refresher & Diagnostic.

docs.title: JS Refresher & Diagnostic
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 1

Scheduled Black Tue, Aug 4, 2026 · Gold Wed, Aug 5, 2026

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Run a JavaScript file with Node from VS Code (set up in Module 0)
  • Confidently use JS fundamentals — variables and scope, types, functions, arrays, and objects — without looking them up
  • Name exactly which fundamentals (if any) you need to shore up before we go advanced
🔑 Why it matters

React is JavaScript. There is no React skill that isn't a JavaScript skill underneath. Shaky fundamentals don't announce themselves — they show up three weeks from now as a React bug that makes no sense. You've written JavaScript before, so most of this is a confirm-and-continue pass. The point isn't to re-learn; it's to find the one or two soft spots and firm them up while it's cheap.

This is a fast module. If the diagnostic goes smoothly, you're done in a day.

📖 Learn (reference, not cover-to-cover)

You know most of this. Use these as targeted reference — only dig in where the diagnostic below trips you up.

Topic Go-to resource Variables, scope, let/const javascript.info: Variables → Code structure Types & type conversion javascript.info: Data types · Type conversions Truthiness & comparisons javascript.info: Comparisons · Logical operators Functions javascript.info: Functions Arrays javascript.info: Arrays Objects javascript.info: Objects

const vs let: in modern JS (and all of React) you use const by default and let only when you must reassign. If you're still reaching for let out of habit, break it now — it matters in React.

⌨️ Practice — The Diagnostic

Do these cold, in a JS file, without looking anything up. Then check yourself against the criteria. Each one names the resource to review if you miss it.

1. Scope & const/let. Predict the output before running it, then run it:

const x = 10;
if (true) {
  const x = 20;
  console.log(x);   // ?
}
console.log(x);     // ?

✅ You can explain block scope and why the two logs differ. (Miss → Variables/scope.)

2. Truthiness. Without running, which of these are truthy?

0, "", "0", [], {}, null, undefined, NaN, "false"

✅ You got all 9 right. [] and "0" and "false" are the tricky truthy ones. (Miss → Comparisons.)

3. Functions three ways. Write the same "add two numbers" function as (a) a function declaration, (b) a function expression, (c) an arrow function.

✅ All three work and you can say one difference between them. (Miss → Functions.)

4. Array basics. Given const nums = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9], write code to:

  • add 4 to the end, then remove the first element
  • get the length
  • check whether it includes 8

✅ Uses push/shift/.length/.includes correctly. (Miss → MDN Array.)

5. Objects. Create an object student with name, grade, and a method describe() that returns "<name> is in grade <grade>". Then read name two ways (dot and bracket).

✅ Method uses this; both access styles work. (Miss → Objects.)

6. Loop + condition. Given an array of numbers, write a loop that logs only the even ones. (Any loop style is fine.)

✅ Correct output; you used % correctly. (Miss → review loops on javascript.info.)

7. The honest one. Which of 1–6 did you have to think hardest about? Write it in your notes — that's your Part 1 focus area.

🔨 Build — The Repair Pass

Your workspace is already set up — Module 0 did Node, VS Code, the capstone folder, and your notes Doc. Nothing new to install.

  1. In your capstone folder, make diagnostic.js and do the cold pass above.
  2. Run it from the VS Code terminal (Ctrl+`): node diagnostic.js
  3. The repair pass. For every item you missed or hesitated on, go to javascript.info, find it, and write in your notes:
    • what you got wrong (or weren't sure about)
    • what's actually correct, in your own words
    • the URL where you found it
  4. Fix your code.

Same URL discipline as Module 0 — finding it yourself in the reference is the skill this course runs on, and a thing you looked up sticks about ten times better than a thing you were told.

Your log entry goes in your notes Doc, under a Module 1 heading — what you built, what confused you and how you resolved it, and any AI use.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • ☐ Say when to use const vs let (and default to const)?
  • ☐ Predict what's truthy and what's falsy?
  • ☐ Write a function three ways and name a difference?
  • ☐ Add/remove array elements and check membership?
  • ☐ Create an object with a method that uses this?
  • ☐ Run a .js file with node and see its output?

If any box is unchecked, spend 20 minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • diagnostic.js runs and covers all six items
  • Your predictions for items 1 and 2 are in your Log — written before you ran anything
  • Every miss is logged: what was wrong, what's correct, and the URL
  • Your focus area is named
  • build check: show me the diagnostic running, walk me through item 1, and tell me which fundamental you want to sharpen. Five minutes. Then start Module 2.

Next: Module 2 — Functions Deep-Dive (arrow functions, callbacks, higher-order functions, closures, this) — where the real React groundwork begins.

docs.title: Modern Syntax & ToolingPart 1 · Module 10 — Modern Syntax & Tooling
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 10

Scheduled Black Thu, Sep 3, 2026 · Gold Fri, Sep 4, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Reach into nested data safely with ?.
  • Supply a fallback with ??, and say how it differs from ||
  • Say what npm install actually did to your folder
  • Scaffold and run a Vite project
  • Have the shell of your P1 Data App running locally
🔑 Why it matters

This is the last module before the project. Two small pieces of syntax that will save you from a specific crash, and the tool every React project in the world is built with.

By the end of this module you should have a Vite dev server running and your Data App's folder in existence. The build block opens next.

IdeaWhere you meet it again ?.Reading API data, where a field you expected is sometimes just not there ??Defaults that survive 0 and "" — a real bug source npmEvery dependency you will ever add, and node_modules finally making sense VitePart 2. Every React project starts with the command you are about to run

Optional chaining is not a style preference. It is what stops "Cannot read properties of undefined" — the single most common runtime error in JavaScript, and the one most likely to break your Data App in front of somebody.

📖 Learn TopicGo-to resource Optional chainingjavascript.info: Optional chaining Nullish coalescingjavascript.info: Nullish coalescing What npm isnpm docs: About npm Vite, start hereVite: Getting Started · Why Vite

Read "Why Vite" even if you skipped it in Module 8. Running a command you do not understand is how tooling becomes superstition, and you will be running this one for the rest of the year.

The one idea underneath all of it

Real data has holes in it.

Your own objects are always complete because you wrote them. Data from an API is missing fields, has nulls where you expected numbers, and changes shape between records. The two operators in this module exist entirely because of that, and everything about the Data App gets easier once you stop assuming the data is tidy.

⌨️ Build — data-app/

Two parts today. First modern.js for the syntax, then a real Vite project that becomes your Data App.

1 · ?. — reading data that has holes in it 
const user = { name: "Ada", address: { city: "London" } };
const other = { name: "Grace" };                 // no address at all

console.log(user.address.city);      // "London"
console.log(other.address.city);     // TypeError — the classic crash
  1. Run it and read the error properly: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'city')
  2. Fix it with other.address?.city and see undefined instead of a crash
  3. Chain deeper: other?.address?.city?.length
  4. Try it on a function that might not exist: obj.method?.()

Done when: You can explain which thing was undefined in the original error — it was address, not city, and reading that correctly is half of debugging.

This is the error you will hit most often for the rest of your life. Learn to read it: the thing in the parentheses is what you were trying to read; the thing that was undefined is what came before the dot.

2 · ?? versus || 
const score = 0;
console.log(score || 100);    // 100  — wrong! 0 is a real score
console.log(score ?? 100);    // 0    — right
  1. Run it and make sure the difference is genuinely clear
  2. Do the same with an empty string "" as a username
  3. Write down the rule: || triggers on falsy, ?? triggers only on null or undefined
  4. Combine them: const city = user?.address?.city ?? "Unknown";

Done when: You can name two values where || gives the wrong answer. 0 and "" are the two that cause real bugs — a score of zero and a blank-but-valid name.

Item 4 is the line you will write a hundred times in Part 2. Reach in safely, fall back sensibly. It is the whole pattern for rendering API data.

3 · What npm actually does 
npm init -y
npm install dayjs
  1. Run both in a scratch folder and then look at what changed
  2. Open package.json and find dayjs in dependencies
  3. Look at node_modules/ — count the folders, and notice it is far more than one
  4. Find package-lock.json and read the first twenty lines
  5. Use it: import dayjs from "dayjs"; console.log(dayjs().format("YYYY-MM-DD"));

Done when: You can say what each of the three artefacts is for: package.json is what you asked for, package-lock.json is exactly what you got, and node_modules is the actual code. And you know why node_modules is never committed.

One install pulled in dozens of folders. Those are your dependency's dependencies. This is worth ten seconds of thought before you add a package for something you could write in five lines.

4 · Your first Vite project 
npm create vite@latest data-app -- --template vanilla
cd data-app
npm install
npm run dev
  1. Run it and open the URL it prints
  2. Edit main.js, save, and watch the browser update without a refresh
  3. Read index.html and find the <script type="module"> line — that is Module 8's work showing up
  4. Stop the server, run npm run build, and look inside dist/

Done when: The dev server hot-reloads, and you have looked inside dist/ and seen that your readable source has become something else entirely. That is the build step the Module 8 stretch was about.

We use the vanilla template deliberately. No React yet — this is your Data App, and Part 2 starts a separate React project. Doing plain JS first means you will know which parts of Part 2 are React and which parts were always just JavaScript.

5 · The shell of your Data App

You have a Vite project. Make it the beginning of the real thing.

  1. Pick your API and write its URL in your log. It must return a list of something
  2. Move your Module 9 fetch function into data-app/src/api.js as a named export
  3. Import it in main.js, call it, and console.log the result
  4. Put one field from the first record onto the page with document.querySelector
  5. Confirm your error handling from M9 came along with it

Done when: Real data from a real API is visible in a browser you are running. It is one field and it is ugly. It is also the project working end to end, which is the hardest part and it is now behind you.

Choose an API that needs no key and allows browser requests. PokeAPI and JSONPlaceholder both work. If yours needs a key or blocks CORS, change it now rather than during the build block.

Stretch · Look at what you shipped
  1. Run npm run build and note the file sizes Vite reports
  2. Open the built JS in dist/assets/ and try to read it
  3. Add dayjs to the project, use it once, rebuild, and compare sizes
  4. Write two sentences: what did one small dependency cost you?

Done when: You have a number for what a dependency costs. That number is why "just npm install it" is a decision rather than a reflex.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • Say what ?. does when the thing before it is undefined?
  • Name two values where || gives the wrong default and ?? does not?
  • Explain the difference between package.json and package-lock.json?
  • Say why node_modules is not committed to git?
  • Say what npm run build produced and why a browser wants it?
  • Name your Data App's API and what it returns?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • modern.js demonstrates ?. and ??, including a case where || is wrong
  • npm run dev serves your data-app and hot-reloads on save
  • Real data from your chosen API is on the page — one field is enough
  • Your M9 error handling survived the move
  • Your log entry is written, including your API's URL and what it returns
  • build check: show me the dev server, the data on the page, and tell me what happens when the API is down. Five minutes.

Next: the P1 Data App build block, opening Sep 9/10 — choose your API and prove the fetch, then render, then loading and error states, then filter and sort, then deploy. Everything from Modules 1 to 10 becomes one thing you can send someone a link to.

docs.title: Functions Deep-Dive
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 2

Scheduled Black Thu, Aug 6, 2026 · Gold Fri, Aug 7, 2026

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Write arrow functions and say what they do differently from function
  • Pass a function to another function as a callback, and write a higher-order function that takes one
  • Explain what a closure is by pointing at one you wrote
  • Predict what this refers to — and explain why an arrow function changes the answer
🔑 Why it matters

Every line of React you write in Part 2 is one of these five ideas wearing a different hat.

In this module In React Callback onClick={handleClick} Higher-order function items.map(item => <li>{item}</li>) Closure useState — the value your component remembers between renders Arrow functions and this Why modern React has no this in it at all A function that returns a function Custom hooks

This is the module where "I already know JavaScript" stops being true for most people. Closures are the wall. Everyone hits it. Hitting it is not a sign you're behind — it's the module working.

This is a two-day module. Module 1 was a sprint; this one has real content.

📖 Learn

Unlike Module 1, you probably do need to read this one. Read the closure article properly — it's the one with the diagram of nested boxes, and the diagram is the whole idea.

Topic Go-to resource Functions as values javascript.info: Function expressions Callbacks javascript.info: Callbacks Arrow functions, the basics javascript.info: Arrow functions Closures javascript.info: Variable scope, closure this in methods javascript.info: Object methods, "this" Arrow functions and this javascript.info: Arrow functions revisited Decorators (for the stretch) javascript.info: Decorators and forwarding The one idea underneath all of it

In JavaScript a function is a value. You can put it in a variable, pass it to another function, return it from a function, and store it in an array.

const shout = (s) => s.toUpperCase();
const alsoShout = shout;          // no parentheses — the function itself
console.log(alsoShout("hey"));    // HEY

The moment you write shout() with parentheses you are no longer passing the function — you're passing whatever it returned. That one character is the most common bug in this module, and it is still the most common bug in professional React code.

⌨️ Build — toolkit.js

In your capstone folder, make toolkit.js. Five parts, in order. Run it as you go with node toolkit.js.

1 · Three ways, then arrows

Take your "add two numbers" function from Module 1 and write it as an arrow function. Then write it again as a one-line arrow with an implicit return (no braces, no return).

✅ Both work, and you can say what the braces changed.

2 · applyTwice(fn, value)

Write a function that takes a function and a value, and returns the result of applying the function to the value twice. applyTwice(x => x * 2, 5) gives 20.

✅ You passed a function as an argument without calling it.

3 · myMap(array, callback) — write map yourself

Write your own version of map: loop over the array, call callback on each element, push the result into a new array, return the new array. Don't use the built-in .map().

Test it: myMap([1, 2, 3], n => n * 10) gives [10, 20, 30].

✅ It returns a new array and leaves the original untouched.

Module 3 is entirely built-in array methods. You will never be confused about what map does, because you'll have written it.

4 · makeCounter() — the closure

Write a function that returns an object with two methods: increment() and get(). The count lives in a variable inside makeCounter, and nothing outside can reach it except through those two methods.

Then make two counters and prove they don't share a number:

const a = makeCounter();
const b = makeCounter();
a.increment(); a.increment(); b.increment();
console.log(a.get(), b.get());   // 2 1

✅ Two independent counts, and you can say where each one is stored.

That's a closure — increment still has access to a variable that, by every rule you know about scope, should be long gone. This is exactly what useState does.

5 · The this trap

Write an object player with name, score, and a method describe() that returns "<name> has <score> points" using this. Confirm it works.

Now rewrite describe as an arrow function and run it again. Record what happens in your notes, then answer: what is this pointing at in the arrow version?

✅ You broke it on purpose, and you can say why it broke.

Stretch · once(fn)

Write a function that takes a function and returns a new function that only ever runs once — after the first call it returns the first result and ignores the arguments. This is a closure and a higher-order function at the same time, and it's a real pattern you'll see in production code.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • ☐ Pass a function to another function without calling it by accident?
  • ☐ Say what makes a function "higher-order"?
  • ☐ Write myMap from scratch?
  • ☐ Point at a closure in your own file and say what it's remembering?
  • ☐ Predict what this is inside a method vs. inside an arrow function?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • toolkit.js runs and covers all five parts
  • Your two counters print independent numbers
  • The broken arrow-function describe() is in your notes with your explanation
  • Your log entry is written — what you built, what confused you and how you resolved it, any AI use, and the URL of anything you looked up
  • build check: run it, walk me through myMap line by line, make a third counter in front of me and tell me why it starts at zero, and show me the this break. Five minutes.

Next: Module 3 — Array Methods (map, filter, reduce, find, some/every) — where you trade myMap for the real one and never write a for loop over data again.

docs.title: Array Methods
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Module 3

Scheduled Black Mon, Aug 10, 2026 · Gold Tue, Aug 11, 2026

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Use map, filter, and reduce to transform data without writing a for loop
  • Say which one to reach for from the shape of the problem
  • Explain why these return new arrays and why that matters
  • Chain them together to answer a real question about a real dataset
🔑 Why it matters

This is the module that shows up in every React file you will ever write.

In this module In React map items.map(item => <li key={item.id}>{item.name}</li>) — rendering a list filter Showing only the results that match a search box reduce A cart total, a count, any summary number Returning a new array The entire reason useState updates work at all

You wrote myMap by hand in Module 2. Now you get the real one — and you will never be confused about what it does, because you built it.

Every one of these is a higher-order function. You already know what that means. That is not a coincidence and it is not a list of methods to memorise; it is one idea you already own, wearing five hats.

📖 Learn

Read the array methods page properly. It is long, and the parts you need are the worked examples — skim the rest.

Topic Go-to resource The whole family javascript.info: Array methods map and filter specifically javascript.info: Array methods — transform reduce javascript.info: reduce/reduceRight Arrays in general, if you need it javascript.info: Arrays

reduce is the hard one. Everyone finds it hard. Read that section twice and do not move on until you have run the worked example yourself.

The one idea underneath all of them

Each of these takes a function and gives you back something new. The original array is never touched.

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

const doubled = nums.map(n => n * 2);      // [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
console.log(nums);                          // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  — unchanged

That "unchanged" is the whole reason React works the way it does. Hold onto it.

Which one do I reach for?

Learn this table by the shape of the question, not by the name:

The question The method What you get back "Turn each item into something else" map A new array, same length "Keep only the ones that match" filter A new array, shorter or equal "Boil the whole thing down to one value" reduce One thing — a number, a string, an object "Find the first one that matches" find One item, or undefined "Is there at least one?" / "Are they all?" some / every true or false

The give-away is the return shape. Same length → map. Fewer → filter. One value → reduce.

⌨️ Build — data.js

In your capstone folder, make data.js. Run it as you go with node data.js.

Start by pasting this dataset in at the top. Everything below uses it.

const games = [
  { title: "Hollow Knight",  year: 2017, hours: 42, price: 15, finished: true  },
  { title: "Celeste",        year: 2018, hours: 12, price: 20, finished: true  },
  { title: "Hades",          year: 2020, hours: 60, price: 22, finished: false },
  { title: "Outer Wilds",    year: 2019, hours: 22, price: 20, finished: true  },
  { title: "Tunic",          year: 2022, hours: 18, price: 30, finished: false },
  { title: "Stardew Valley", year: 2016, hours: 95, price: 15, finished: false },
];
1 · map — three transformations

Produce, each on its own line:

  1. An array of just the titles
  2. An array of "Celeste (2018)"-style strings
  3. An array of the prices with 10% off, as numbers

✅ Three new arrays. Print games afterwards and confirm it is untouched.

2 · filter — three questions
  1. Games you have finished
  2. Games with more than 20 hours played
  3. Games released after 2018 that cost under $25 — one filter, two conditions

✅ Each result is shorter than the original, and the original still has six items.

3 · reduce — the hard one

Do these in order. Do not skip to the third one.

const totalHours = games.reduce((sum, game) => sum + game.hours, 0);

Run that first and make sure you can say what sum and 0 are doing.

  1. Total hours across all games (the line above — type it, don't paste it)
  2. Total money spent
  3. The game with the most hours, using reduce — not sort

✅ You can explain what the second argument to reduce is for.

The 0 is the starting value. Leave it off and reduce uses the first item instead, which is fine for numbers and breaks in confusing ways for objects. Try it both ways on #1 and see.

4 · find, some, every 
const firstUnfinished = games.find(g => !g.finished);
const anyExpensive    = games.some(g => g.price > 28);
const allPlayed       = games.every(g => g.hours > 10);

Then answer in your notes: what does find return when nothing matches, and why is that different from what filter returns?

✅ You can say why find gives you an item and filter gives you an array.

5 · Chain them

One expression, no intermediate variables:

"The total hours I've spent on games I haven't finished."

const wastedHours = games
  .filter(/* ... */)
  .reduce(/* ... */);

Then one more: the titles of every finished game released before 2019, alphabetised.

✅ You chained at least three methods and the original games array is still intact.

Stretch · groupBy

Write a function that takes the array and a key name, and returns an object grouping the games by that key:

groupBy(games, "finished");
// { true: [ ...3 games ], false: [ ...3 games ] }

This is reduce building an object instead of a number, and it is the moment reduce stops feeling like a weird way to add things up.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • ☐ Say which method to use from the shape of the question?
  • ☐ Write a map that produces a formatted string?
  • ☐ Write a filter with two conditions?
  • ☐ Explain what reduce's second argument does?
  • ☐ Say why find returns an item but filter returns an array?
  • ☐ Chain a filter into a reduce?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • data.js runs and covers all five parts
  • games is unchanged at the end — print it and prove it
  • Your chained expression works in one statement
  • Your log entry is written — what you built, what confused you and how you resolved it, any AI use, and the URL of anything you looked up
  • build check: run it, walk me through your reduce line by line, and tell me which method you'd reach for if I asked you a question you haven't seen. Five minutes.

Next: Module 4 — ES6+ Syntax (destructuring, spread, template literals, default parameters) — the syntax that makes all of today's code shorter, and that you will see in every React tutorial ever written.
