<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>Quake Watch</title>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>
<header>
  <h1>Quake Watch</h1>
  <p>Every earthquake recorded worldwide in the last 24 hours, from the USGS.</p>
</header>
<main id="output">
  <!-- main.js fills this: loading, then the list, or an error with a retry button -->
</main>
<footer>
  <p>Data from the <a href="https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/">USGS Earthquake Feed</a>.</p>
</footer>
<!-- type="module" is what makes import/export work in the browser. Without it
     you get "Cannot use import statement outside a module". -->
<script type="module" src="src/main.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
src/api.js 
// api.js — everything that talks to the network lives here, and nothing else does.
//
// Splitting this out is requirement 7 (ES modules). It also makes the app
// testable: main.js can be handed a fake fetch and never touch the internet.

const FEED = "https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/all_day.geojson";

/**
 * Turns whatever went wrong into a sentence a human can act on.
 * A thrown TypeError from fetch means the request never left the building.
 */
export function describeError(err) {
  if (err instanceof TypeError) return "Could not reach the server. Check your connection.";
  if (err.status === 404) return "That feed does not exist any more.";
  if (err.status >= 500) return "The server is having a bad day. Try again in a minute.";
  if (err.status) return `The server refused the request (${err.status}).`;
  return "Something went wrong loading the data.";
}

/**
 * The shape the rest of the app wants, pulled out of the feed's shape.
 * Stage 4 keeps a few more fields for the detail view. `?.` and `??` are
 * doing real work here: the feed genuinely has holes in it.
 */
export function toQuakes(geojson) {
  return geojson.features.map((f) => {
    const [lon, lat, depth] = f.geometry?.coordinates ?? [];
    return {
      id: f.id,
      magnitude: f.properties.mag,
      place: f.properties.place,
      time: f.properties.time,
      url: f.properties.url,
      depth,                                   // km below the surface
      felt: f.properties.felt ?? 0,            // "did you feel it?" reports
      tsunami: f.properties.tsunami === 1,
      lat,
      lon,
    };
  });
}

/**
 * Fetch the feed and hand back plain objects.
 * `doFetch` is a seam for testing — production passes nothing and gets real fetch.
 */
export async function loadQuakes(doFetch = fetch) {
  const response = await doFetch(FEED);
  if (!response.ok) {
    // A 404 is a SUCCESSFUL request for a page that isn't there. fetch does not
    // throw on it, which surprises everyone exactly once.
    const err = new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    err.status = response.status;
    throw err;
  }
  return toQuakes(await response.json());
}
src/main.js 
// main.js — wires the pieces together. This file makes decisions; the others do not.
import { loadQuakes, describeError } from "./api.js";
import { applyControls, findQuake } from "./quakes.js";
import { renderLoading, renderError, renderControls, renderList, renderDetail } from "./render.js";

const output = document.querySelector("#output");

// ALL of the app's state, in one place. Everything on screen is a function of this.
const state = {
  quakes: [],                                        // what the API gave us, never mutated
  controls: { minMagnitude: 0, query: "", sortBy: "time" },
  selectedId: null,                                  // a detail view is open when this is set
};

async function load() {
  // The loading state goes up BEFORE the await, or nobody ever sees it.
  renderLoading(output);
  try {
    state.quakes = await loadQuakes();
    renderApp();
  } catch (err) {
    renderError(output, describeError(err));
    document.querySelector("#retry")?.addEventListener("click", load);
  }
}

/** Two regions: controls are drawn once, results are redrawn on every change. */
function renderApp() {
  output.innerHTML = `<section id="controls" class="controls"></section><section id="results"></section>`;
  renderControls(document.querySelector("#controls"), state.controls);
  renderResults();
}

function renderResults() {
  const results = document.querySelector("#results");
  const controls = document.querySelector("#controls");
  if (state.selectedId) {
    controls.hidden = true;
    renderDetail(results, findQuake(state.quakes, state.selectedId));
  } else {
    controls.hidden = false;
    renderList(results, applyControls(state.quakes, state.controls), { total: state.quakes.length });
  }
}

/** Read the three controls into state, then redraw only the results. */
function onControlsChanged() {
  state.controls = {
    minMagnitude: Number(document.querySelector("#min-magnitude").value) || 0,
    query: document.querySelector("#search").value,
    sortBy: document.querySelector("#sort").value,
  };
  renderResults();
}

// One listener on the container instead of one per row (event delegation):
// rows come and go with every re-render, the container does not.
output.addEventListener("input", (e) => {
  if (e.target.closest("#controls")) onControlsChanged();
});
output.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const open = e.target.closest("[data-id]");
  if (open) {
    state.selectedId = open.dataset.id;
    renderResults();
  } else if (e.target.id === "back") {
    state.selectedId = null;
    renderResults();
  }
});

load();
src/quakes.js 
// quakes.js — the pure logic. Arrays in, arrays out. No fetch, no DOM.
//
// This is requirement 5 (filter / sort / search with array methods), and it is
// the file the Node harness can test without a browser, because nothing in
// here knows a browser exists.

/** Keep only quakes at or above a magnitude. A missing magnitude counts as 0. */
export function filterByMinMagnitude(quakes, min) {
  return quakes.filter((q) => (q.magnitude ?? 0) >= min);
}

/** Case-insensitive match on the place name. An empty search keeps everything. */
export function searchByPlace(quakes, text) {
  const needle = text.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (needle === "") return quakes;
  return quakes.filter((q) => (q.place ?? "").toLowerCase().includes(needle));
}

/**
 * A NEW array, ordered. `sort` mutates whatever you call it on, so the copy
 * (`[...quakes]`) is the whole point of this function — without it the
 * "original" list quietly changes order underneath the app.
 */
export function sortQuakes(quakes, key) {
  const sorted = [...quakes];
  if (key === "magnitude") {
    sorted.sort((a, b) => (b.magnitude ?? -Infinity) - (a.magnitude ?? -Infinity));
  } else {
    sorted.sort((a, b) => b.time - a.time);        // newest first
  }
  return sorted;
}

/** The three above, in the order the UI applies them. One call from main.js. */
export function applyControls(quakes, { minMagnitude = 0, query = "", sortBy = "time" } = {}) {
  return sortQuakes(searchByPlace(filterByMinMagnitude(quakes, minMagnitude), query), sortBy);
}

/** The record behind a click, or null. The detail view is a lookup, not a second fetch. */
export function findQuake(quakes, id) {
  return quakes.find((q) => q.id === id) ?? null;
}
src/render.js 
// render.js — everything that touches the DOM lives here.
//
// Each function takes the element to write into. None of them fetch anything,
// and none of them decide anything. That separation is why they are testable.

export function renderLoading(el) {
  el.innerHTML = `<p class="state">Loading earthquakes…</p>`;
}

export function renderError(el, message) {
  el.innerHTML = `<p class="state error">${message}</p>
    <button id="retry" type="button">Try again</button>`;
}

export function renderEmpty(el) {
  el.innerHTML = `<p class="state">No earthquakes in the last day. Genuinely good news.</p>`;
}

/** Different from "no data": there is data, the controls just exclude all of it. */
export function renderNoMatches(el) {
  el.innerHTML = `<p class="state">Nothing matches. Lower the minimum magnitude or clear the search.</p>`;
}

/** Magnitude to a CSS class, so the styling is data-driven rather than hard-coded. */
export function severity(magnitude) {
  if (magnitude >= 5) return "major";
  if (magnitude >= 3) return "moderate";
  return "minor";
}

/**
 * The controls are rendered ONCE, at load. Re-rendering them on every
 * keystroke would replace the input the user is typing in, and the focus goes
 * with it. main.js re-renders the results only.
 */
export function renderControls(el, controls) {
  el.innerHTML = `
    <label>Min magnitude
      <input id="min-magnitude" type="number" min="0" max="10" step="0.5" value="${controls.minMagnitude}">
    </label>
    <label>Search place
      <input id="search" type="search" placeholder="e.g. Alaska" value="${controls.query}">
    </label>
    <label>Sort by
      <select id="sort">
        <option value="time" ${controls.sortBy === "time" ? "selected" : ""}>Newest first</option>
        <option value="magnitude" ${controls.sortBy === "magnitude" ? "selected" : ""}>Strongest first</option>
      </select>
    </label>`;
}

export function renderList(el, quakes, { total = quakes.length } = {}) {
  if (total === 0) return renderEmpty(el);
  if (quakes.length === 0) return renderNoMatches(el);
  el.innerHTML = `<ul class="quakes">` + quakes.map((q) => `
    <li class="quake ${severity(q.magnitude)}">
      <span class="mag">${q.magnitude?.toFixed(1) ?? "?"}</span>
      <button class="place" type="button" data-id="${q.id}">${q.place ?? "Unknown location"}</button>
      <time datetime="${new Date(q.time).toISOString()}">${new Date(q.time).toLocaleTimeString()}</time>
    </li>`).join("") + `</ul>
    <p class="count">${quakes.length} of ${total} in the last 24 hours</p>`;
}

/** Requirement 6: one item, in full. The Back button is handled by main.js. */
export function renderDetail(el, q) {
  if (!q) return renderNoMatches(el);
  el.innerHTML = `
    <article class="detail ${severity(q.magnitude)}">
      <button id="back" type="button">← Back to the list</button>
      <h2><span class="mag">${q.magnitude?.toFixed(1) ?? "?"}</span> ${q.place ?? "Unknown location"}</h2>
      <dl>
        <dt>When</dt><dd>${new Date(q.time).toLocaleString()}</dd>
        <dt>Depth</dt><dd>${q.depth == null ? "unknown" : `${q.depth.toFixed(1)} km`}</dd>
        <dt>Location</dt><dd>${q.lat?.toFixed(2) ?? "?"}, ${q.lon?.toFixed(2) ?? "?"}</dd>
        <dt>Felt reports</dt><dd>${q.felt}</dd>
        <dt>Tsunami warning</dt><dd>${q.tsunami ? "yes" : "no"}</dd>
      </dl>
      <p><a href="${q.url}" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Full USGS event page</a></p>
    </article>`;
}

docs.title: P1 Data App — Loading & error states
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Work block

Scheduled Black Tue, Sep 15, 2026 · Gold Wed, Sep 16, 2026

Today's learning target

I can show a loading state, catch a failed request, and tell the user something useful instead of showing a blank page.

What your app does when the network is slow, or gone, or the API has moved.

This is a work block, not a module. There is no new lecture — you are building Project 1. The requirement numbers below point at the Project 1 checklist, which is laid out in full on the first work block page, Choose your API and prove the fetch.

What to get done
  1. Add renderLoading(el) and call it before the await, not after. After the await, nobody ever sees it.
  2. Wrap the fetch in try / catch.
  3. Check response.ok and throw yourself. A 404 is a successful request for a page that is not there — fetch does not throw on it, and this surprises everyone exactly once.
  4. Write a function that turns an error into a sentence a person can act on. “Check your connection” is useful; TypeError: Failed to fetch is not.
  5. Add a Try again button in the error state.
  6. Test all three states. Turn your wifi off and reload. Point at a URL that does not exist. Throttle the network in DevTools to see your own loading state.
Done when
  • A loading state appears before the data does
  • Wifi off, reload — a readable message, not a blank page and not a crash
  • A bad URL gives a different message from being offline
  • Try again actually retries
  • You have seen all three states with your own eyes, not just written the code
If you are stuck

The 404 behaviour is the concept of the day: fetch only rejects when the request never happened. A 404 or a 500 resolves normally with ok === false, so an app without that check renders undefined and looks broken for no visible reason. Requirements 2 and 3 on the Project 1 checklist are exactly this.

Before you leave

Commit and push. A work block you cannot get back to is a work block you did not have.

docs.title: P1 Data App — Polish, responsive, README
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Work block

Scheduled Black Mon, Sep 21, 2026 · Gold Tue, Sep 22, 2026

Today's learning target

I can make my app hold up on a phone, read cleanly to a stranger, and explain itself in a README.

The difference between a thing that works and a thing you would show someone.

This is a work block, not a module, and today is subtraction: no new features. Everything on this list makes the app you already have hold up better. The requirement numbers point at the Project 1 checklist on the first work block page, Choose your API and prove the fetch.

What to get done
  1. Open DevTools, device toolbar, 375 px wide. Fix everything that overflows, overlaps, or needs a horizontal scroll. One @media (max-width: 480px) block and flex-wrap on the controls fix most of it.
  2. Hunt every undefined, NaN, and null the user can see. A missing field gets a fallback with ??. Put the formatting of dates, numbers, and units in one small module so the same value reads the same way everywhere.
  3. Dead code: unused functions, commented-out blocks, console.logs. Delete them. const unless something is reassigned. Rename anything a stranger could not read. Requirement 8.
  4. Keyboard and focus: Tab through the page. Every control reachable, focus visible, the detail view's Back button a real <button>.
  5. Write README.md: one sentence saying what it is, the API and its URL, how to run it, a file table saying what each file does, and the nine-requirement checklist with where each one is met. Leave a Live: line for Wednesday.
  6. Read the whole app top to bottom once, as the person grading it. Fix what embarrasses you.
Done when
  • Nothing overflows at 375 px, and there is no horizontal scroll
  • No undefined, NaN, or null is visible anywhere, including the detail view of your ugliest record
  • No console.log, no commented-out code, no unused function, no let that could be const
  • Tab reaches every control and you can see where you are
  • README.md opens with what it is, and someone else could run the app from it
  • The README's checklist names a file for each of the nine requirements
If you are stuck

Polish is mostly subtraction. If the list is long, order it by what a stranger notices first: a broken layout on a phone, then a visible undefined, then a README that does not say what the thing is. The formatting module is the one addition that pays for itself — three different date formats on one page is the most common thing a grader notices and the cheapest thing to fix.

Before you leave

Commit and push. A work block you cannot get back to is a work block you did not have.

</head>
<body>
<header>
  <h1>Quake Watch</h1>
  <p>Every earthquake recorded worldwide in the last 24 hours, from the USGS.</p>
</header>
<main id="output">
  <!-- main.js fills this: loading, then the controls and the list, or an error with a retry button -->
</main>
<footer>
  <p>Data from the <a href="https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/">USGS Earthquake Feed</a>. Times are shown in your local time zone.</p>
</footer>
<!-- type="module" is what makes import/export work in the browser. Without it
     you get "Cannot use import statement outside a module". The path is
     relative (no leading slash) so it still resolves when the site is served
     from a sub-folder, which GitHub Pages does. -->
<script type="module" src="./src/main.js"></script>

src/api.js 
// api.js — everything that talks to the network lives here, and nothing else does.
//
// Splitting this out is requirement 7 (ES modules). It also makes the app
// testable: main.js can be handed a fake fetch and never touch the internet.

const FEED = "https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/all_day.geojson";

/**
 * Turns whatever went wrong into a sentence a human can act on.
 * A thrown TypeError from fetch means the request never left the building.
 */
export function describeError(err) {
  if (err instanceof TypeError) return "Could not reach the server. Check your connection.";
  if (err.status === 404) return "That feed does not exist any more.";
  if (err.status >= 500) return "The server is having a bad day. Try again in a minute.";
  if (err.status) return `The server refused the request (${err.status}).`;
  return "Something went wrong loading the data.";
}

/**
 * The shape the rest of the app wants, pulled out of the feed's shape.
 * Stage 4 keeps a few more fields for the detail view. `?.` and `??` are
 * doing real work here: the feed genuinely has holes in it.
 */
export function toQuakes(geojson) {
  return geojson.features.map((f) => {
    const [lon, lat, depth] = f.geometry?.coordinates ?? [];
    return {
      id: f.id,
      magnitude: f.properties.mag,
      place: f.properties.place,
      time: f.properties.time,
      url: f.properties.url,
      depth,                                   // km below the surface
      felt: f.properties.felt ?? 0,            // "did you feel it?" reports
      tsunami: f.properties.tsunami === 1,
      lat,
      lon,
    };
  });
}

/**
 * Fetch the feed and hand back plain objects.
 * `doFetch` is a seam for testing — production passes nothing and gets real fetch.
 */
export async function loadQuakes(doFetch = fetch) {
  const response = await doFetch(FEED);
  if (!response.ok) {
    // A 404 is a SUCCESSFUL request for a page that isn't there. fetch does not
    // throw on it, which surprises everyone exactly once.
    const err = new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    err.status = response.status;
    throw err;
  }
  return toQuakes(await response.json());
}
src/format.js 
// format.js — how a value reads on the page, decided once.
//
// Stage 5 pulled these out of render.js because the same date was being
// formatted three different ways in three places. Every "?" and "unknown" the
// user can see comes from here, so a missing field never shows as undefined.

export function formatMagnitude(magnitude) {
  return typeof magnitude === "number" ? magnitude.toFixed(1) : "?";
}

export function formatDepth(km) {
  return typeof km === "number" ? `${km.toFixed(1)} km` : "unknown";
}

export function formatCoords(lat, lon) {
  if (typeof lat !== "number" || typeof lon !== "number") return "unknown";
  return `${lat.toFixed(2)}, ${lon.toFixed(2)}`;
}

/** Clock time for the list; the detail view wants the full date as well. */
export function formatTime(ms, { full = false } = {}) {
  const d = new Date(ms);
  return full ? d.toLocaleString() : d.toLocaleTimeString([], { hour: "2-digit", minute: "2-digit" });
}
src/main.js 
// main.js — wires the pieces together. This file makes decisions; the others do not.
import { loadQuakes, describeError } from "./api.js";
import { applyControls, findQuake } from "./quakes.js";
import { renderLoading, renderError, renderControls, renderList, renderDetail } from "./render.js";

const output = document.querySelector("#output");

// ALL of the app's state, in one place. Everything on screen is a function of this.
const state = {
  quakes: [],                                        // what the API gave us, never mutated
  controls: { minMagnitude: 0, query: "", sortBy: "time" },
  selectedId: null,                                  // a detail view is open when this is set
};

async function load() {
  // The loading state goes up BEFORE the await, or nobody ever sees it.
  renderLoading(output);
  try {
    state.quakes = await loadQuakes();
    renderApp();
  } catch (err) {
    renderError(output, describeError(err));
    document.querySelector("#retry")?.addEventListener("click", load);
  }
}

/** Two regions: controls are drawn once, results are redrawn on every change. */
function renderApp() {
  output.innerHTML = `<section id="controls" class="controls"></section><section id="results"></section>`;
  renderControls(document.querySelector("#controls"), state.controls);
  renderResults();
}

function renderResults() {
  const results = document.querySelector("#results");
  const controls = document.querySelector("#controls");
  if (state.selectedId) {
    controls.hidden = true;
    renderDetail(results, findQuake(state.quakes, state.selectedId));
  } else {
    controls.hidden = false;
    renderList(results, applyControls(state.quakes, state.controls), { total: state.quakes.length });
  }
}

/** Read the three controls into state, then redraw only the results. */
function onControlsChanged() {
  state.controls = {
    minMagnitude: Number(document.querySelector("#min-magnitude").value) || 0,
    query: document.querySelector("#search").value,
    sortBy: document.querySelector("#sort").value,
  };
  renderResults();
}

// One listener on the container instead of one per row (event delegation):
// rows come and go with every re-render, the container does not.
output.addEventListener("input", (e) => {
  if (e.target.closest("#controls")) onControlsChanged();
});
output.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const open = e.target.closest("[data-id]");
  if (open) {
    state.selectedId = open.dataset.id;
    renderResults();
  } else if (e.target.id === "back") {
    state.selectedId = null;
    renderResults();
  }
});

load();
src/quakes.js 
// quakes.js — the pure logic. Arrays in, arrays out. No fetch, no DOM.
//
// This is requirement 5 (filter / sort / search with array methods), and it is
// the file the Node harness can test without a browser, because nothing in
// here knows a browser exists.

/** Keep only quakes at or above a magnitude. A missing magnitude counts as 0. */
export function filterByMinMagnitude(quakes, min) {
  return quakes.filter((q) => (q.magnitude ?? 0) >= min);
}

/** Case-insensitive match on the place name. An empty search keeps everything. */
export function searchByPlace(quakes, text) {
  const needle = text.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (needle === "") return quakes;
  return quakes.filter((q) => (q.place ?? "").toLowerCase().includes(needle));
}

/**
 * A NEW array, ordered. `sort` mutates whatever you call it on, so the copy
 * (`[...quakes]`) is the whole point of this function — without it the
 * "original" list quietly changes order underneath the app.
 */
export function sortQuakes(quakes, key) {
  const sorted = [...quakes];
  if (key === "magnitude") {
    sorted.sort((a, b) => (b.magnitude ?? -Infinity) - (a.magnitude ?? -Infinity));
  } else {
    sorted.sort((a, b) => b.time - a.time);        // newest first
  }
  return sorted;
}

/** The three above, in the order the UI applies them. One call from main.js. */
export function applyControls(quakes, { minMagnitude = 0, query = "", sortBy = "time" } = {}) {
  return sortQuakes(searchByPlace(filterByMinMagnitude(quakes, minMagnitude), query), sortBy);
}

/** The record behind a click, or null. The detail view is a lookup, not a second fetch. */
export function findQuake(quakes, id) {
  return quakes.find((q) => q.id === id) ?? null;
}
src/render.js 
// render.js — everything that touches the DOM lives here.
//
// Each function takes the element to write into. None of them fetch anything,
// and none of them decide anything. That separation is why they are testable.
import { formatMagnitude, formatDepth, formatCoords, formatTime } from "./format.js";

export function renderLoading(el) {
  el.innerHTML = `<p class="state" role="status">Loading earthquakes…</p>`;
}

export function renderError(el, message) {
  el.innerHTML = `<p class="state error" role="alert">${message}</p>
    <button id="retry" type="button">Try again</button>`;
}

export function renderEmpty(el) {
  el.innerHTML = `<p class="state">No earthquakes in the last day. Genuinely good news.</p>`;
}

/** Different from "no data": there is data, the controls just exclude all of it. */
export function renderNoMatches(el) {
  el.innerHTML = `<p class="state">Nothing matches. Lower the minimum magnitude or clear the search.</p>`;
}

/** Magnitude to a CSS class, so the styling is data-driven rather than hard-coded. */
export function severity(magnitude) {
  if (magnitude >= 5) return "major";
  if (magnitude >= 3) return "moderate";
  return "minor";
}

/**
 * The controls are rendered ONCE, at load. Re-rendering them on every
 * keystroke would replace the input the user is typing in, and the focus goes
 * with it. main.js re-renders the results only.
 */
export function renderControls(el, controls) {
  el.innerHTML = `
    <label>Min magnitude
      <input id="min-magnitude" type="number" min="0" max="10" step="0.5" value="${controls.minMagnitude}">
    </label>
    <label>Search place
      <input id="search" type="search" placeholder="e.g. Alaska" value="${controls.query}">
    </label>
    <label>Sort by
      <select id="sort">
        <option value="time" ${controls.sortBy === "time" ? "selected" : ""}>Newest first</option>
        <option value="magnitude" ${controls.sortBy === "magnitude" ? "selected" : ""}>Strongest first</option>
      </select>
    </label>`;
}

export function renderList(el, quakes, { total = quakes.length } = {}) {
  if (total === 0) return renderEmpty(el);
  if (quakes.length === 0) return renderNoMatches(el);
  el.innerHTML = `<ul class="quakes">` + quakes.map((q) => `
    <li class="quake ${severity(q.magnitude)}">
      <span class="mag">${formatMagnitude(q.magnitude)}</span>
      <button class="place" type="button" data-id="${q.id}">${q.place ?? "Unknown location"}</button>
      <time datetime="${new Date(q.time).toISOString()}">${formatTime(q.time)}</time>
    </li>`).join("") + `</ul>
    <p class="count">${quakes.length} of ${total} in the last 24 hours</p>`;
}

/** Requirement 6: one item, in full. The Back button is handled by main.js. */
export function renderDetail(el, q) {
  if (!q) return renderNoMatches(el);
  el.innerHTML = `
    <article class="detail ${severity(q.magnitude)}">
      <button id="back" type="button">← Back to the list</button>
      <h2><span class="mag">${formatMagnitude(q.magnitude)}</span> ${q.place ?? "Unknown location"}</h2>
      <dl>
        <dt>When</dt><dd>${formatTime(q.time, { full: true })}</dd>
        <dt>Depth</dt><dd>${formatDepth(q.depth)}</dd>
        <dt>Location</dt><dd>${formatCoords(q.lat, q.lon)}</dd>
        <dt>Felt reports</dt><dd>${q.felt}</dd>
        <dt>Tsunami warning</dt><dd>${q.tsunami ? "yes" : "no"}</dd>
      </dl>
      <p><a href="${q.url}" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Full USGS event page</a></p>
    </article>`;
}
styles.css 
:root { color-scheme: light; }
* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body {
  margin: 0 auto; max-width: 46rem; padding: 2rem 1rem 4rem;
  font: 16px/1.6 -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Arial, sans-serif;
  color: #14161a; background: #fbfaf7;
}
h1 { margin: 0 0 .2rem; }
header p { color: #5b6270; margin: 0 0 2rem; }
footer { margin-top: 3rem; color: #5b6270; font-size: .85em; }
a { color: #1d4ed8; }

/* states */
.state { padding: 1rem; background: #eff0f2; border-radius: 6px; }
.state.error { background: #fdeae3; border-left: 4px solid #d1491f; }

/* every focusable thing shows focus — keyboard users exist */
button, input, select { font: inherit; }
button { padding: .5rem 1rem; margin-top: .6rem; cursor: pointer; }
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #1d4ed8; outline-offset: 2px; }

/* the controls row wraps instead of overflowing on a narrow screen */
.controls { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; margin-bottom: 1rem; }
.controls label { display: flex; flex-direction: column; font-size: .85em; color: #5b6270;
                  flex: 1 1 10rem; }
.controls input, .controls select { padding: .35rem .5rem; width: 100%; }

/* the list */
.quakes { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; }
.quake { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 3.2rem 1fr auto; gap: .8rem;
         align-items: baseline; padding: .55rem .6rem; border-bottom: 1px solid #e2e0da; }
.mag { font-weight: 800; text-align: right; }
.minor .mag { color: #6b7280; }
.moderate .mag { color: #b45309; }
.major .mag { color: #b3261e; }
time { color: #6b7280; font-size: .85em; white-space: nowrap; }
.count { color: #5b6270; font-size: .9em; }

/* a row's place name is a button, styled to read as a link */
.place { margin: 0; padding: 0; border: 0; background: none; text-align: left;
         color: #1d4ed8; text-decoration: underline; overflow-wrap: anywhere; }

/* the detail view */
.detail dl { display: grid; grid-template-columns: max-content 1fr; gap: .3rem 1rem; }
.detail dt { color: #5b6270; }
.detail dd { margin: 0; }

/* phones: the row stacks, the time drops under the place */
@media (max-width: 480px) {
  body { padding: 1.25rem .9rem 3rem; }
  .quake { grid-template-columns: 3rem 1fr; }
  .quake time { grid-column: 2; }
  .detail dl { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
  .detail dd { margin-bottom: .5rem; }
}

docs.title: P1 Data App — Render real data to the page
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P1 JavaScript for React · Work block

Scheduled Black Fri, Sep 11, 2026 · Gold Mon, Sep 14, 2026

Today's learning target

I can turn an API response into DOM elements, with the fetching and the drawing in separate modules.

The JSON dump becomes a list a person would want to look at.

This is a work block, not a module. There is no new lecture — you are building Project 1. The requirement numbers below point at the Project 1 checklist, which is laid out in full on the first work block page, Choose your API and prove the fetch.

What to get done
  1. Write a function that maps the raw response into the shape your UI wants — just the fields you will show, flat.
  2. Put that in api.js. Put the drawing in a new render.js. Nothing in render.js fetches; nothing in api.js touches the DOM.
  3. Write renderList(el, items) that builds the markup and writes it once.
  4. Style it enough to be readable. This is not the styling block, but a wall of unstyled text hides real problems.
  5. Handle the empty case: what does the page say when the list has zero items?
Done when
  • The page shows a real list, not JSON
  • api.js never touches the DOM; render.js never fetches
  • The mapped objects hold only the fields you actually display
  • An empty list produces a sentence, not a blank page
  • You build the markup once and assign it once, rather than in a loop
If you are stuck

Two things to watch. Building the DOM inside a loop with += on innerHTML re-parses the whole list every pass; build a string or an array first and assign it once. And it is tempting to fetch inside render.js because it is convenient — that is the module boundary collapsing on day one. Keep the fetch in api.js.

Before you leave

Commit and push. A work block you cannot get back to is a work block you did not have.

docs.title: Setup & JSXPart 2 · Module 1 — Setup & JSX
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P2 React.js · Module 1

Scheduled Black Tue, Sep 29, 2026 · Gold Wed, Sep 30, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Scaffold a React project with Vite and say what each generated file is for
  • Read a .jsx file and say which parts are HTML-shaped and which are JavaScript
  • Write a component: a capitalised function that returns JSX
  • Put a JavaScript value into JSX with { }, and know why it is className
  • Explain what Vite does to JSX before a browser ever sees it
🔑 Why it matters

Part 2 starts here, and it starts from the app you just shipped. Project 2 is Project 1 rebuilt in React and made bigger. This module builds the shell of that rebuild: a React project that draws your app's page with hard-coded data. No fetch yet, no state yet. Just the page, in JSX.

Everything you did in Part 1 comes with you. npm create vite@latest is Module 10's command with one word changed. ES modules are Module 8. The functions you write today are Module 2's functions. React is a library, not a new language.

IdeaWhere you meet it again A component is a functionEvery module from here on. Module 2 gives them props JSX is JavaScriptModule 5, when .map() builds the list inside the markup Vite compiles JSXModule 9, when the build is what gets deployed 📖 Learn TopicGo-to resource Start herereact.dev: Quick Start — the first page, all of it JSX, properlyreact.dev: Writing Markup with JSX Values inside JSXreact.dev: JavaScript in JSX with Curly Braces Your first componentreact.dev: Your First Component Vite + ReactVite: Getting Started — the scaffolding section

Read Writing Markup with JSX with the three rules in front of you: return a single root, close every tag, camelCase almost everything. Every JSX error you get this week is one of those three.

The one idea underneath all of it

JSX is not HTML. It is JavaScript that looks like HTML.

<h1>{title}</h1> is a function call in disguise. Vite turns it into one before the browser sees it, which is why you can put any JavaScript expression inside the braces, why class has to be className (it is a reserved word in JavaScript), and why a component has to return one thing (a function returns one value). Once that is clear, every JSX rule is a consequence rather than a rule.

⌨️ Build — capstone/

One project, capstone/. Keep it next to your Part 1 app, not inside it. It is the Project 2 repo from today.

1 · Scaffold it, and read every file 
npm create vite@latest capstone -- --template react
cd capstone
npm install
npm run dev
  1. Open the URL it prints. Click the counter. That is state, and it is Module 3 — ignore it for now
  2. Read index.html. Find the one <div id="root"> and the <script type="module">
  3. Read src/main.jsx. createRoot takes that div; .render(<App />) puts the app inside it. Every React app starts with these five lines
  4. Read src/App.jsx. Find the function, find the return, find the markup inside the return
  5. Look at package.json: react and react-dom are the dependencies; vite and the React plugin are dev dependencies. Say what the difference is

Done when: You can say what each of the four files does, in one sentence each, and you know why the template says --template react where Module 10 said --template vanilla.

The dev server hot-reloads. Keep it running in a terminal all module. Save a file, look at the browser. If the browser goes white, the error is in the terminal and in the browser overlay — read it, it names the file and the line.

2 · Break JSX three ways, on purpose

In App.jsx, one at a time, then undo each:

  1. Return two sibling elements with no wrapper. Read the error: Adjacent JSX elements must be wrapped
  2. Write <br> without the slash. Read the error
  3. Write class="x" instead of className="x". It runs — now read the warning in the console

Done when: You have seen all three messages and can say which rule each one is enforcing: one root, every tag closed, camelCase attributes. The fix for the first is a fragment, <>…</>, and you know why it exists.

3 · Your app's page, in JSX

Delete everything inside App's return, and the counter code above it. Then rebuild your Part 1 app's page, with hard-coded data:

  1. The header: your app's title and tagline. Put both in consts above the return and use {title} in the markup
  2. Three list items, typed out by hand, showing the same fields your Part 1 list shows. Three, not thirty — .map() is Module 5
  3. At least one value computed in braces: a .toFixed(1), a date formatted with toLocaleTimeString, a string built with a template literal
  4. A {/* comment */} inside the markup explaining why it is className
  5. Copy your Part 1 styles.css over the generated index.css, and delete App.css and the import of it. The class names match, so the page should look like your Part 1 app

Done when: The browser shows your Part 1 app's page — header, three rows, footer — drawn by React from App.jsx, styled by your own stylesheet, and every piece of text in it came through a { } or a JSX tag you wrote.

Nothing here fetched anything. That is deliberate. Module 1 is about the shape of a component. When the fetch comes back in Module 6, the markup you wrote today is what it fills.

4 · Build it, and look at what JSX became 
npm run build
  1. Open dist/assets/. Find the JS file. Search it for your app's title
  2. Notice there is no <h1> anywhere near it — the JSX is gone. Find the function call that replaced it (it will mention jsx or createElement)
  3. Note the size of that file. Most of it is React itself; the number is what Project 2's deploy will ship

Done when: You have seen, in the built file, that your JSX became function calls. That is the whole answer to “why do I need Vite to run this” and it is the exit ticket.

Stretch · Write the function call yourself
  1. In App.jsx, add import { createElement } from "react";
  2. Replace one element — the footer's paragraph — with createElement("p", null, "Data from …")
  3. Confirm the page is identical. Then put the JSX back and write two sentences about why nobody writes it the long way

Done when: You have written one element without JSX and it rendered. JSX is now a convenience you understand rather than syntax you obey.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • Name the three JSX rules and the error each one produces when broken?
  • Say why it is className and not class?
  • Say what createRoot(…).render(<App />) does, and where root comes from?
  • Say what a fragment is for?
  • Say what Vite did to App.jsx before the browser got it?
  • Say which two packages are dependencies and which are dev dependencies, and why the split?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • capstone/ is a Vite + React project that runs with npm run dev and builds with npm run build
  • App.jsx draws your Part 1 app's page from hard-coded data, styled by your own stylesheet
  • At least one value in the markup is computed inside { }
  • The template's counter, logo, and App.css are gone
  • Your log entry is written, including what JSX became in dist/
  • build check: show me the dev server, then point at any tag in App.jsx and tell me what Vite turns it into. Five minutes.

Next: Module 2 — Components & Props. The one big return you wrote today gets cut into pieces, and the data every piece needs travels down to it as props.

docs.title: Components & PropsPart 2 · Module 2 — Components & Props
docs.text:
7253 Software Development Capstone · P2 React.js · Module 2

Scheduled Black Thu, Oct 1, 2026 · Gold Tue, Oct 20, 2026

7253 Software Development Capstone · self-guided · work at your own pace

🎯 Objective

By the end of this module you can:

  • Cut one big component into small ones, each in its own file
  • Pass data into a component as props, and read it with destructuring
  • Say which way data flows in React, and what a child can and cannot do with a prop
  • Use children to build a component that wraps whatever is put inside it
  • Draw your app's component tree, and say what each node needs to be given
🔑 Why it matters

A React app is a tree of components, and props are how data moves down it. Module 1's App was one big return; a real app is dozens of small functions, each responsible for one piece of the page, each told what to draw by whoever renders it.

This module is where Project 2's requirement 1 lives — broken into multiple components with props — and it is the module the Project 2 proposal is built on. The component sketch you draw here is the one you submit before Module 3.

IdeaWhere you meet it again Props flow downModule 3, when state lives in a parent and props carry it to children One row component, many rowsModule 5: quakes.map((q) => <Row {...} />) childrenModule 7, layout and composition patterns The component treeThe Project 2 proposal, and Module 7's “where should this state live” 📖 Learn TopicGo-to resource Components, importing and exportingreact.dev: Importing and Exporting Components Propsreact.dev: Passing Props to a Component — all of it, including children Destructuring, if it is rustyjavascript.info: Destructuring assignment (Module 4) Thinking in treesreact.dev: Thinking in React — steps 1 and 2 only, for now

Passing Props to a Component is the page. Read it with a file open and type the examples. The sections on default values, spreading, and children are all used below.

The one idea underneath all of it

Data flows one way: down. A prop is read-only.

A parent decides what a child gets, and the child draws it. The child cannot change the prop, and it cannot reach up and change the parent. That one restriction is what makes a React app predictable: to know why a row looks the way it does, you look at what its parent passed it, and nothing else. Every hard React bug you meet later will come from something trying to get around this.

⌨️ Build — capstone/

Still capstone/, still hard-coded data. By the end, App.jsx is short and the page is a tree.

1 · The header becomes a component
  1. Make src/components/Header.jsx. Move the <header> markup into a function called Header, export default it
  2. Give it two props: function Header({ title, tagline }). Use them in the markup
  3. In App.jsx: import Header from "./components/Header.jsx"; and render <Header title="…" tagline="…" />
  4. Change the title in App.jsx and watch it change on the page. The data lives in the parent

Done when: The header is drawn by a component in its own file, from two props passed by App, and you can say why the parameter is written ({ title, tagline }) and not (title, tagline) — props arrive as one object.

2 · One row component, drawn three times
  1. Make src/components/Row.jsx (or a name that fits your data — MovieCard, PokemonRow). Move one <li> into it
  2. Everything that differs between rows becomes a prop: function Row({ magnitude, place, time }). Numbers go in braces: magnitude={5.2}; strings can be quoted
  3. Render it three times in App with different props. Delete the other two hand-typed <li>s
  4. Move any plain JavaScript the row needs — your severity banding, a formatter — into a plain .js file under src/ and import it. It has no JSX and imports nothing from React
  5. Delete one prop from one <Row /> and look at the page. Then give that prop a default: place = "Unknown location"

Done when: Three rows on the page, one Row function, and a missing prop shows a default rather than nothing. You can say why magnitude="5.2" (quoted) would break .toFixed().

Three explicit <Row />s, not a .map(). You can see the map coming; that is Module 5, and it needs key, which is its own lesson. Today the point is that one function draws many rows.

3 · A component that wraps things: children
  1. Make src/components/Callout.jsx: function Callout({ children }) returning <p className="callout">{children}</p>
  2. Use it in App with text between the tags: <Callout>Three rows, from props.</Callout>
  3. Put an element inside it instead of text — a <code>, a <strong>. Then another component. It renders whatever it is given
  4. Add a second prop with a default, kind = "info", that changes the class. Render one <Callout kind="warn">
  5. Add the .callout style to your stylesheet

Done when: Callout renders text, elements, and other components without knowing which, and you can say where children came from — React fills it with whatever sits between the opening and closing tags.

4 · Read-only, and one way
  1. Inside Row, try magnitude = magnitude + 1; before the return. Read what happens (with destructuring it is a local variable and the parent is untouched; the page does not change)
  2. Try to change App's title from inside Header. There is no way to. Write down why that is a feature
  3. Open React DevTools (the browser extension) and click a Row. Read its props on the right

Done when: You have tried to push data upward and could not, and you can say in one sentence what that buys you when something on the page looks wrong.

5 · Draw your tree

On paper or in your log. Your Part 1 app, as React components:

  1. Every component as a box: App, Header, the list, the row, the controls, the detail view, the error and loading states
  2. An arrow from each parent to each child, labelled with the props that travel along it
  3. A star on every box that will need data that changes — the search text, the selected item, the loaded list. Those are Module 3's problem; today you are only finding them

Done when: The tree exists, every arrow has props on it, and the starred boxes are the ones you would have to explain in your Project 2 proposal. Photograph it into your log.

Stretch · Spread, and the shape of a prop
  1. Put one row's data in an object and render <Row {...quake} />. Say what the spread did
  2. Pass the whole object as one prop instead, <Row quake={quake} />, and change Row to match. Which is better, and when?
  3. Read Thinking in React step 3 and mark, on your tree, the “minimal state”

Done when: You can argue both sides of “one object prop vs several props” and you have picked one for your app on purpose.

✅ Check Yourself

Can you, without looking anything up:

  • Say which way data flows in React, and what a child can do with a prop?
  • Write a component signature that takes two props, with a default for one?
  • Say what children is and who fills it?
  • Say why count="3" and count={3} are different?
  • Point at your tree and say which boxes hold data that changes?
  • Say what an export default and a default import have to do with each other?

If any box is unchecked, spend twenty minutes on that row's resource. Then check it.

🏁 Done When
  • App.jsx renders Header, three Rows and at least one Callout, each in its own file under src/components/
  • Every difference between rows is a prop; a missing prop shows a default
  • The plain-JavaScript helpers live in a .js file with no React in it
  • Your component tree is drawn, arrows labelled with props, changing data starred
  • Your log entry is written, including the one-sentence answer to “why can't a child change a prop”
  • build check: show me the tree on the page and the tree on paper, then delete a prop from one row and tell me what will happen before you save. Five minutes.

Next: Module 3 — State: useState, on Oct 19 (Black) / Oct 21 (Gold). The starred boxes on your tree get their data, and the Project 2 proposal is due before it opens.

docs.title: 7183 Principles of Computing
docs.text:
Godot and Python game programming - the pathway's on-ramp.

The on-ramp to the pathway. Semester 1 builds four games in Godot 4 with GDScript, each one introducing the programming ideas the next one depends on. Semester 2 moves to Python and Pygame with the same project-first approach.

No prior programming experience is assumed. You will write code on day one.

Java and JavaFX in semester 1, Python and the PCEP certification in semester 2.

Semester 2 switches to Python and works toward the PCEP-30-02 certification, an industry credential you sit for in this class.

/*
 * U1 L1 — HELLO COMPILER · STARTER CODE
 * 7184 Software Development · Unit 1, Lesson 1
 *
 * This is the first file of your arena game. Every lesson in this unit adds to
 * THIS file — by Lesson 5 it takes input and prints a formatted status line.
 *
 * TO RUN IT — two separate commands, on purpose:
 *
 *     javac Main.java      compiles it. This MAKES Main.class
 *     java Main            runs the .class file. No .java on the end
 *
 * Do them one at a time at least once today. The first command makes the
 * program, the second one runs it. That split is the whole point of Lesson 1,
 * and it is the thing Python never made you think about.
 */
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        // Done for you, so you can compile and run before you change anything.
        System.out.println("The arena awaits.");


        // TODO 1: three more lines that open YOUR game.
        //         Not an arena unless you want one — a dungeon, a spaceship,
        //         a haunted kitchen. One System.out.println("..."); per line.
        //         Compile and run after EACH line, not at the end.


        // TODO 2: an empty line in the output. System.out.println("");


        // TODO 3: break it on purpose. Do these ONE AT A TIME, and read the
        //         error out loud before you undo it:
        //
        //           a) delete a semicolon
        //           b) change  System.out.println  to  system.out.println
        //           c) delete one closing quote "
        //
        //         javac gives you a line number and a reason. Three different
        //         mistakes, three different messages. Learning to read them now
        //         is worth more than anything else you do today.

    }
}

src/Main.java
/*
 * U1 L10 — METHODS, PARAMETERS, RETURN VALUES · STARTER CODE
 * 7184 Software Development · Unit 1, Lesson 10
 *
 * ALREADY HERE:  Lessons 1-9 finished. It works. It is also 258 lines long
 *                and every one of them is inside main.
 * YOU'RE ADDING: nothing. Today you MOVE things.
 *
 *     javac Main.java
 *     java Main
 *
 * THE RULE OF THE DAY: BEHAVIOUR MUST NOT CHANGE.
 *
 *   1. Run it now. Play one fight. Write down what happens.
 *   2. Refactor.
 *   3. Run it again. If anything is different, you broke it.
 *
 * That discipline has a name — refactoring — and it is worth more than the
 * syntax you learn today.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * YOUR TARGET
 *
 *   main right now:  258 lines
 *   main by the end: under 60
 *
 * Count it before and after. Both numbers go on the board.
 * ==========================================================================
 *
 * HOW TO DO THIS WITHOUT BREAKING IT
 *
 *   Move ONE thing. Compile. Run. Then move the next one.
 *
 *   Moving six methods and then compiling gives you six errors at once and no
 *   idea which change caused which. Moving one gives you one.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * THE ORDER TO WORK IN — easiest first, so you get a win early
 *
 * TODO 1: the pure-output ones. No return value; nothing to get subtly wrong.
 *
 *           static void printBanner(String text) {
 *               System.out.println("=".repeat(40));
 *               System.out.printf("  %s%n", text);
 *           }
 *
 *           static void printHealthBar(int hp) { ... }
 *           static void printTitle() { ... }
 *           static void countdown(int from) { ... }
 *
 *         Methods go at CLASS level — as siblings of main, not inside it.
 *         Look at where main's closing brace is and put them after it.
 *
 * TODO 2: the ones that hand a value back.
 *
 *           static boolean isAlive(int hp) {
 *               return hp > 0;
 *           }
 *
 *           static int calculateDamage(int power, int roll) {
 *               if (roll >= 9) return power * 2;
 *               if (roll >= 3) return power;
 *               return 0;
 *           }
 *
 *           static int applyDamage(int hp, int damage) { return hp - damage; }
 *
 *         Three returns in one method is fine. The first one that runs wins.
 *
 * TODO 3: the arena. It is the biggest single block in main and it moves
 *         without changing a character:
 *
 *           static void drawArena(int playerRow, int playerCol,
 *                                 int enemyRow, int enemyCol) { ... }
 *
 *         It needs FOUR parameters because a method cannot see main's local
 *         variables. That is not a limitation to work around — it is the
 *         entire point. The method works for any positions you hand it.
 *
 * TODO 4: the big win — the input validation from Lesson 8.
 *
 *           static int readChoice(Scanner in, int min, int max) {
 *               int choice;
 *               do {
 *                   System.out.printf("Choose %d-%d: ", min, max);
 *                   while (!in.hasNextInt()) {
 *                       in.next();
 *                       System.out.printf("Numbers only. Choose %d-%d: ", min, max);
 *                   }
 *                   choice = in.nextInt();
 *                   in.nextLine();
 *               } while (choice < min || choice > max);
 *               return choice;
 *           }
 *
 *         Twelve lines you fought for in Lesson 8, now one call — and you can
 *         use it anywhere you need a number in a range. THAT is abstraction.
 *
 * TODO 5: OVERLOAD calculateDamage with a crit-multiplier version.
 *
 *           static int calculateDamage(int power, int roll, double critMultiplier)
 *
 *         Same name, different PARAMETER LIST. Two methods that differ only in
 *         return type will not compile — try it once so you see the error.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * THE ONE THAT WILL CATCH YOU
 *
 *   static void tryToHeal(int hp) { hp += 50; }   // does NOTHING
 *
 *   Java hands the method a COPY. Changing the copy does not change yours.
 *   The fix is to give it back:
 *
 *       health = heal(health, 50);
 *
 *   When a method "does nothing", this is why. Every time.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * FINISHED EARLY?
 *
 *   Extract the entire enemy turn into one method.
 *
 *   You will find you need several values back — the enemy's health, the
 *   damage dealt, whether it is still standing — and there is only one
 *   return. Sit with that for five minutes.
 *
 *   You want to return a whole FIGHTER. In Unit 2 you will.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * WHAT TO SUBMIT — THIS IS CHECKPOINT 1
 *
 *   Back up as Arena_CP1_LastnameF and submit it on Canvas.
 *   Your game must behave exactly as it did this morning.
 */

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Your Lesson 9 file goes below, unchanged. Start from YOUR OWN code — the
// point of today is refactoring what you wrote, not typing something new.
//
// If you have lost your L9 work, ask, and start from the L9 solution instead.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

import java.util.Scanner;

public class Main {

    static final int MAX_HEALTH = 100;
    static final int STARTING_GOLD = 20;
    static final int ROWS = 5;
    static final int COLS = 11;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("""
                ========================
                     THE ARENA
                ========================
                """);
        System.out.println("Sand, torchlight, and a crowd that has already decided how this ends.");
        System.out.println("The gate opens.");
        System.out.println("");

        System.out.print("What is your name, challenger? ");
        String playerName = in.nextLine().trim();
        if (playerName.isEmpty()) {
            playerName = "Challenger";
        }

        int difficulty;
        do {
            System.out.print("Difficulty (1 = easy, 2 = normal, 3 = brutal): ");
            while (!in.hasNextInt()) {
                System.out.print("Numbers only. Try again: ");
                in.next();
            }
            difficulty = in.nextInt();
        } while (difficulty < 1 || difficulty > 3);
        in.nextLine();

        String difficultyName = switch (difficulty) {
            case 1 -> "Easy";
            case 2 -> "Normal";
            case 3 -> "Brutal";
            default -> "Unknown";
        };
        System.out.println("Difficulty: " + difficultyName);
        System.out.println("");

        int health = MAX_HEALTH;
        int potions = 2;
        int playerRow = 2, playerCol = 1;
        int enemyRow = 2, enemyCol = 9;

        String enemyName = "Cave Goblin";
        int enemyHealth = 30 + difficulty * 15;
        int enemyPower = 4 + difficulty * 3;

        System.out.printf("%-12s HP %3d/%3d  Gold %4d  Lv %d%n",
                          playerName, health, MAX_HEALTH, STARTING_GOLD, 1);
        System.out.println("");

        System.out.printf("%s enters the arena. The %s has %d HP.%n",
                          playerName, enemyName, enemyHealth);
        System.out.print("Press Enter to begin...");
        in.nextLine();
        System.out.println("");

        for (int i = 3; i > 0; i--) {
            System.out.println(i + "...");
        }
        System.out.println("FIGHT!");
        System.out.println("");

        int turnNumber = 1;
        boolean playing = true;
        boolean fled = false;

        while (playing) {
            System.out.println("=".repeat(40));
            System.out.printf("  Turn %d%n", turnNumber);
            System.out.printf("%-12s HP %3d/%3d    %-14s HP %3d%n",
                              playerName, health, MAX_HEALTH, enemyName, enemyHealth);
            System.out.println("");

            for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
                for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
                    if (r == playerRow && c == playerCol)      System.out.print('@');
                    else if (r == enemyRow && c == enemyCol)   System.out.print('X');
                    else if (r == 0 || r == ROWS - 1)          System.out.print('-');
                    else if (c == 0 || c == COLS - 1)          System.out.print('|');
                    else                                       System.out.print(' ');
                }
                System.out.println();
            }
            System.out.println("");

            boolean adjacent = (playerRow == enemyRow) && (Math.abs(playerCol - enemyCol) == 1);
            int roll = (turnNumber * 3) % 10 + 1;
            int damage = 0;

            if (adjacent) {
                System.out.print("[A]ttack  [D]efend  [P]otion  [L]eft  [R]ight  [F]lee: ");
            } else {
                System.out.print("The " + enemyName + " is out of reach.  "
                                 + "[L]eft  [R]ight  [D]efend  [P]otion  [F]lee: ");
            }
            String action = in.nextLine().trim().toUpperCase();

            switch (action) {
                case "A" -> {
                    if (!adjacent) {
                        System.out.println("You swing at empty air. Get closer first.");
                    } else if (roll >= 9) {
                        damage = enemyPower * 2;
                        System.out.println("CRITICAL HIT!");
                    } else if (roll >= 3) {
                        damage = enemyPower;
                        System.out.println("A solid hit.");
                    } else {
                        System.out.println("You miss.");
                    }
                }
                case "L" -> {
                    if (playerCol - 1 < 1) {
                        System.out.println("The wall stops you.");
                    } else {
                        playerCol--;
                        System.out.println("You step left.");
                    }
                }
                case "R" -> {
                    if (playerCol + 1 > COLS - 2) {
                        System.out.println("The wall stops you.");
                    } else if (playerCol + 1 == enemyCol) {
                        System.out.println("The " + enemyName + " blocks your way.");
                    } else {
                        playerCol++;
                        System.out.println("You step right.");
                    }
                }
                case "D" -> {
                    health += 5;
                    System.out.println("You raise your guard and recover 5 HP.");
                }
                case "P" -> {
                    if (potions > 0) {
                        potions--;
                        health += 25;
                        System.out.println("You drink a potion and recover 25 HP.");
                    } else {
                        System.out.println("You reach for a potion. There are none.");
                    }
                }
                case "F" -> {
                    fled = true;
                    System.out.println("You run for the gate. The crowd howls.");
                }
                default -> System.out.println("The crowd jeers. You hesitate and lose the turn.");
            }

            enemyHealth -= damage;

            if (!fled && enemyHealth > 0 && adjacent) {
                health -= enemyPower;
                System.out.printf("The %s strikes back for %d.%n", enemyName, enemyPower);
            }

            if (health > MAX_HEALTH) {
                health = MAX_HEALTH;
            } else if (health < 0) {
                health = 0;
            }

            int bars = health / 5;
            String bar = "#".repeat(bars) + "-".repeat(20 - bars);
            System.out.printf("[%s] %d%%%n", bar, health);

            if (fled) {
                System.out.println("You escape with your life, and nothing else.");
                playing = false;
            } else if (enemyHealth <= 0) {
                System.out.printf("%nThe %s falls! You win on turn %d.%n", enemyName, turnNumber);
                playing = false;
            } else if (health <= 0) {
                System.out.printf("%nYou have fallen on turn %d.%n", turnNumber);
                playing = false;
            }

            turnNumber++;
        }

        System.out.printf("%nThe arena empties after %d turns.%n", turnNumber - 1);
    }
}

/*
 * U1 L11 — ARRAYS AND 2D GAME BOARDS · STARTER CODE
 * 7184 Software Development · Unit 1, Lesson 11
 *
 * ALREADY HERE:  Lesson 10's refactor. Everything is in methods and it works.
 * YOU'RE ADDING: arrays. A pack that holds items, and an arena that is STORED
 *                rather than drawn from a pile of if-statements.
 *
 *     javac Main.java
 *     java Main
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * THE SHIFT, IN TWO WORDS
 *
 *   Lesson 9  DREW the grid  — a nested loop decided each character
 *   Today you STORE the grid — a char[][] holds the world
 *
 * Everything today follows from that. A hazard becomes one assignment instead
 * of another else-if. Collision becomes reading the cell you are moving into.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * THREE FACTS THAT CAUSE EVERY ARRAY BUG
 *
 *   1. Fixed size at creation. new String[5] is five forever.
 *   2. .length is a FIELD, no parentheses -- unlike string.length().
 *      That inconsistency is Java's fault, not yours. It still catches people.
 *   3. Indices run 0 to length-1. An array of 5 has no index 5.
 *
 *   Defaults: int[] -> 0, boolean[] -> false, String[] -> NULL.
 *   That last one is why NullPointerException is about to happen to you.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * TODO 1: the pack — two arrays, side by side.
 *
 *           String[] itemNames = new String[5];
 *           int[] itemCounts = new int[5];
 *           int itemSlots = 0;
 *
 *           itemNames[0] = "Potion";  itemCounts[0] = 2;  itemSlots++;
 *           itemNames[1] = "Bomb";    itemCounts[1] = 1;  itemSlots++;
 *
 *         Then a method to show it:
 *
 *           static void printInventory(String[] names, int[] counts, int slots)
 *
 *         Loop to `slots`, NOT to names.length. The rest of the array is still
 *         null, and calling anything on null throws.
 *
 *         Then ask yourself: what happens if you sort the names and forget the
 *         counts? Two arrays kept in step BY HAND. Sit with that -- in Unit 2
 *         these become one array of Item objects and the problem disappears.
 *
 * TODO 2: ***THE BOARD***. This is the lesson.
 *
 *           char[][] arena = new char[5][11];
 *
 *           for (int r = 0; r < arena.length; r++) {
 *               for (int c = 0; c < arena[r].length; c++) {
 *                   boolean edge = (r == 0 || r == arena.length - 1
 *                                || c == 0 || c == arena[r].length - 1);
 *                   arena[r][c] = edge ? '#' : ' ';
 *               }
 *           }
 *           arena[playerRow][playerCol] = '@';
 *           arena[enemyRow][enemyCol]   = 'X';
 *
 *         arena.length     = how many ROWS
 *         arena[r].length  = how many COLUMNS in row r
 *
 *         Drawing is now three lines, because a 2D array is an array of rows:
 *
 *           static void drawArena(char[][] arena) {
 *               for (char[] row : arena) {
 *                   System.out.println(new String(row));
 *               }
 *           }
 *
 * TODO 3: movement is now THREE steps, every time:
 *
 *           1. clear the old cell:  arena[r][c] = ' ';
 *           2. update the position
 *           3. set the new cell:    arena[r][c] = '@';
 *
 *         Miss step 1 and your player leaves a trail of '@' behind it. You
 *         will see it immediately and it is funny. Then fix it.
 *
 *         COLLISION is just checking what is already in the cell you are about
 *         to enter. Write a peek(arena, row, col) that returns that character,
 *         then refuse to move into '#' or 'X'.
 *
 * TODO 4: a damage log and its average.
 *
 *           int[] damageLog = new int[20];
 *           ...
 *           int total = 0;
 *           for (int d : damageLog) total += d;
 *           double average = (double) total / damageLog.length;
 *
 *         The cast is Lesson 3's. Leave it out and every average is a whole
 *         number.
 *
 * TODO 5: BREAK IT ON PURPOSE. Twice, deliberately.
 *
 *           inventory[5]        on a 5-length array
 *              -> ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 5
 *
 *           names[3].length()   on a slot you never assigned
 *              -> NullPointerException
 *
 *         Read both messages out loud. Java's array errors are unusually good
 *         -- the first one tells you the index AND the length, which is the
 *         whole diagnosis.
 *
 * ==========================================================================
 * FINISHED EARLY?
 *
 *   Add a hazard '^' that hurts you and a treasure '$' that pays you.
 *   One line each -- because the grid now STORES the world instead of just
 *   drawing it. That is the entire argument for the 2D array.
 *
 * BEFORE YOU LEAVE: back up as Arena_U1L11_LastnameF and submit.
 */

import java.util.Scanner;

/*
 * U1 L10 — METHODS, PARAMETERS, RETURN VALUES · your Lesson 10 code
 *
 * SAME GAME. SAME BEHAVIOUR. Every output is byte-for-byte what L9 produced.
 * The only thing that changed is where the code lives.
 *
 *   main in L9:  258 lines   (measured, not estimated)
 *   main here:    50 lines   -- an 80% cut, into 31 named methods
 *
 * Those numbers are the lesson. Put both on the board.
 *
 * WHY NOT LOWER? The turn switch mutates five things at once -- health,
 * potions, playerCol, damage and fled. Extracting it would need to return all
 * five, and there is only one return. THAT is the extension, and it is the
 * cliffhanger into U2: you want to return a whole fighter, and you cannot yet.
 */
public class Main {

    static final int MAX_HEALTH = 100;
    static final int STARTING_GOLD = 20;
    static final int ROWS = 5;
    static final int COLS = 11;

    // ================= main: the shape of the program, and nothing else =====
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);

        printTitle();
        String playerName = readName(in);
        int difficulty = readChoice(in, 1, 3, "Difficulty (1 = easy, 2 = normal, 3 = brutal)");
        System.out.println("Difficulty: " + difficultyName(difficulty));
        System.out.println("");

        int health = MAX_HEALTH, potions = 2, playerCol = 1;
        final int playerRow = 2, enemyRow = 2, enemyCol = 9;
        String enemyName = "Cave Goblin";
        int enemyHealth = 30 + difficulty * 15;
        int enemyPower = 4 + difficulty * 3;

        openingCeremony(in, playerName, health, enemyName, enemyHealth);

        int turnNumber = 1;
        boolean playing = true, fled = false;

        while (playing) {
            drawTurn(turnNumber, playerName, health, enemyName, enemyHealth,
                     playerRow, playerCol, enemyRow, enemyCol);

            boolean adjacent = isAdjacent(playerRow, playerCol, enemyRow, enemyCol);
            int roll = (turnNumber * 3) % 10 + 1;
            String action = readAction(in, adjacent, enemyName);
            int damage = 0;

            switch (action) {
                case "A" -> damage = attack(adjacent, enemyPower, roll);
                case "L" -> playerCol = moveLeft(playerCol);
                case "R" -> playerCol = moveRight(playerCol, enemyCol, enemyName);
                case "D" -> health = defend(health);
                case "P" -> {
                    if (potions > 0) { potions--; health = drinkPotion(health); }
                    else System.out.println("You reach for a potion. There are none.");
                }
                case "F" -> fled = flee();
                default -> System.out.println("The crowd jeers. You hesitate and lose the turn.");
            }

            enemyHealth = applyDamage(enemyHealth, damage);
            health = enemyResponse(fled, adjacent, health, enemyHealth, enemyPower, enemyName);
            printHealthBar(health);

            playing = !endOfFight(fled, health, enemyHealth, enemyName, turnNumber);
            turnNumber++;
        }

        System.out.printf("%nThe arena empties after %d turns.%n", turnNumber - 1);
    }

    // ================= output: no return value, nothing to get wrong ========

    static void printTitle() {
        System.out.print("""
                ========================
                     THE ARENA
                ========================
                """);
        System.out.println("Sand, torchlight, and a crowd that has already decided how this ends.");
        System.out.println("The gate opens.");
        System.out.println("");
    }

    static void openingCeremony(Scanner in, String name, int hp, String enemy, int enemyHp) {
        printStatus(name, hp, MAX_HEALTH, STARTING_GOLD, 1);
        System.out.printf("%s enters the arena. The %s has %d HP.%n", name, enemy, enemyHp);
        System.out.print("Press Enter to begin...");
        in.nextLine();
        System.out.println("");
        countdown(3);
        System.out.println("");
    }

    static void drawTurn(int turnNumber, String name, int hp, String enemy, int enemyHp,
                         int playerRow, int playerCol, int enemyRow, int enemyCol) {
        printBanner("Turn " + turnNumber);
        printFighters(name, hp, enemy, enemyHp);
        drawArena(playerRow, playerCol, enemyRow, enemyCol);
    }

    static void printBanner(String text) {
        System.out.println("=".repeat(40));
        System.out.printf("  %s%n", text);
    }

    static void printStatus(String name, int hp, int maxHp, int gold, int level) {
        System.out.printf("%-12s HP %3d/%3d  Gold %4d  Lv %d%n", name, hp, maxHp, gold, level);
        System.out.println("");
    }

    static void printFighters(String name, int hp, String enemy, int enemyHp) {
        System.out.printf("%-12s HP %3d/%3d    %-14s HP %3d%n", name, hp, MAX_HEALTH, enemy, enemyHp);
        System.out.println("");
    }

    static void printHealthBar(int hp) {
        int bars = hp / 5;
        System.out.printf("[%s] %d%%%n", "#".repeat(bars) + "-".repeat(20 - bars), hp);
    }

    static void countdown(int from) {
        for (int i = from; i > 0; i--) {
            System.out.println(i + "...");
        }
        System.out.println("FIGHT!");
    }

    // L9's nested loop, unchanged — just moved somewhere with a name.
    static void drawArena(int playerRow, int playerCol, int enemyRow, int enemyCol) {
        for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
                if (r == playerRow && c == playerCol)      System.out.print('@');
                else if (r == enemyRow && c == enemyCol)   System.out.print('X');
                else if (r == 0 || r == ROWS - 1)          System.out.print('-');
                else if (c == 0 || c == COLS - 1)          System.out.print('|');
                else                                       System.out.print(' ');
            }
            System.out.println();
        }
        System.out.println("");
    }

    // ================= input =================

    static String readName(Scanner in) {
        System.out.print("What is your name, challenger? ");
        String name = in.nextLine().trim();
        return name.isEmpty() ? "Challenger" : name;
    }

    // The twelve ugly lines from L8, now one call. THIS is the extraction that
    // makes the case for methods better than any definition does.
    static int readChoice(Scanner in, int min, int max, String prompt) {
        int choice;
        do {
            System.out.printf("%s: ", prompt);
            while (!in.hasNextInt()) {
                in.next();
                System.out.printf("Numbers only. %s: ", prompt);
            }
            choice = in.nextInt();
            in.nextLine();
        } while (choice < min || choice > max);
        return choice;
    }

    static String readAction(Scanner in, boolean adjacent, String enemyName) {
        if (adjacent) {
            System.out.print("[A]ttack  [D]efend  [P]otion  [L]eft  [R]ight  [F]lee: ");
        } else {
            System.out.print("The " + enemyName + " is out of reach.  "
                             + "[L]eft  [R]ight  [D]efend  [P]otion  [F]lee: ");
        }
        return in.nextLine().trim().toUpperCase();
    }

    // ================= things that give a value back =================

    static String difficultyName(int difficulty) {
        return switch (difficulty) {
            case 1 -> "Easy";
            case 2 -> "Normal";
            case 3 -> "Brutal";
            default -> "Unknown";
        };
    }

    static boolean isAlive(int hp) {
        return hp > 0;
    }

    static boolean isAdjacent(int r1, int c1, int r2, int c2) {
        return r1 == r2 && Math.abs(c1 - c2) == 1;
    }

    static int calculateDamage(int power, int roll) {
        if (roll >= 9) return power * 2;
        if (roll >= 3) return power;
        return 0;
    }

    // OVERLOAD: same name, different parameter list. Java picks by what you pass.
    // Note the parameters differ — a return-type-only difference will not compile.
    static int calculateDamage(int power, int roll, double critMultiplier) {
        if (roll >= 9) return (int) (power * critMultiplier);
        if (roll >= 3) return power;
        return 0;
    }

    static int applyDamage(int hp, int damage) {
        return hp - damage;
    }

    static int clamp(int value, int min, int max) {
        return Math.max(min, Math.min(max, value));
    }

    static int attack(boolean adjacent, int enemyPower, int roll) {
        if (!adjacent) {
            System.out.println("You swing at empty air. Get closer first.");
            return 0;
        }
        int damage = calculateDamage(enemyPower, roll);
        if (damage == 0)                   System.out.println("You miss.");
        else if (damage > enemyPower)      System.out.println("CRITICAL HIT!");
        else                               System.out.println("A solid hit.");
        return damage;
    }

    static int moveLeft(int playerCol) {
        if (playerCol - 1 < 1) {
            System.out.println("The wall stops you.");
            return playerCol;
        }
        System.out.println("You step left.");
        return playerCol - 1;
    }

    static int moveRight(int playerCol, int enemyCol, String enemyName) {
        if (playerCol + 1 > COLS - 2) {
            System.out.println("The wall stops you.");
            return playerCol;
        }
        if (playerCol + 1 == enemyCol) {
            System.out.println("The " + enemyName + " blocks your way.");
            return playerCol;
        }
        System.out.println("You step right.");
        return playerCol + 1;
    }

    static int defend(int health) {
        System.out.println("You raise your guard and recover 5 HP.");
        return health + 5;
    }

    static int drinkPotion(int health) {
        System.out.println("You drink a potion and recover 25 HP.");
        return health + 25;
    }

    static boolean flee() {
        System.out.println("You run for the gate. The crowd howls.");
        return true;
    }

    // The enemy only answers if you are still here and it can reach you.
    // Returns the player's new health, clamped — because a method that changes
    // a parameter changes only its own copy.
    static int enemyResponse(boolean fled, boolean adjacent, int health,
                             int enemyHealth, int enemyPower, String enemyName) {
        if (!fled && isAlive(enemyHealth) && adjacent) {
            health = applyDamage(health, enemyPower);
            System.out.printf("The %s strikes back for %d.%n", enemyName, enemyPower);
        }
        return clamp(health, 0, MAX_HEALTH);
    }

    static boolean endOfFight(boolean fled, int health, int enemyHealth,
                              String enemyName, int turnNumber) {
        if (fled) {
            System.out.println("You escape with your life, and nothing else.");
            return true;
        }
        if (!isAlive(enemyHealth)) {
            System.out.printf("%nThe %s falls! You win on turn %d.%n", enemyName, turnNumber);
            return true;
        }
        if (!isAlive(health)) {
            System.out.printf("%nYou have fallen on turn %d.%n", turnNumber);
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}
